topics.title: COST MODEL FOR ANALYSIS / RECORD OPERATIONS

questions.prompt: In this lecture's cost model, what do P and R denote, respectively?
options: The number of data pages and the number of records per page
The number of records and the number of pages per record
The number of index levels and the number of root pages
The number of buffer frames and the number of query operators
questions.explanation: P counts the file's data pages. R measures records per page, rather than the total number of records.

questions.prompt: What does the I/O-only model temporarily ignore?
options: The number of pages in the file
CPU costs, prefetching, and differences between random and sequential I/O
Every page read
Every page write
questions.explanation: The model retains page-I/O costs while simplifying other factors so that broad performance trends can be compared.

questions.prompt: How many matches does the analysis assume for an equality search on a key?
options: Every record matches
There are as many matches as pages
Exactly one match exists
There is never a match
questions.explanation: Assuming that one match exists allows the expected search cost to be approximated by half a file scan. Searching for a missing key has a different cost.

questions.prompt: A uniformly full file has P=200 and R=40. How many records does it contain?
questions.explanation: Multiply pages by records per page: 200×40=8000 records. Adding quantities with different units would not give a record count.

questions.prompt: Why should assumptions be stated before comparing heap and sorted files?
options: A cost formula is meaningful only under its stated conditions
Stating assumptions always makes the cache warm
Every formula is independent of the workload
Equal P values guarantee equal wall-clock times
questions.explanation: A model is an approximation with a defined scope. Files with the same page count can still have different workloads and layouts.

questions.prompt: A heap file has P=120 pages and D=3 ms per page, with no caching. What is the full-scan cost in the I/O-only model?
options: 40 ms
360 ms
180 ms
123 ms
questions.explanation: All 120 pages must be read at 3 ms each, giving 360 ms. The half-file approximation applies to finding one existing key, not to a full scan.

questions.prompt: An existing key is equally likely to be on any of P=9 pages. What is the exact expected number of pages read?
questions.explanation: The average of positions 1 through 9 is (9+1)/2=5. P/2=4.5 is only an approximation.

questions.prompt: How many pages must usually be scanned to find all matches on a non-key attribute in a heap without an index or cache?
options: log₂P
P
questions.explanation: Matching records can occur on any page. Finding one match is not enough to stop when all matches are required.

questions.prompt: Assuming insertion appends to the last page, which I/Os does a heap insertion require?
options: Read the last page and write it back, costing approximately 2D
Only read the last page, costing D
Perform a binary search and shift half the file
Scan all pages and then sort the entire file
questions.explanation: This model assumes the append location is known and ignores other management overhead. Maintaining a sorted file would require a different analysis.

questions.prompt: What approximate cost does the lecture give for deleting an existing key from a heap?
options: log₂P·D
P·D/2 + D
P·D/2
2P·D
questions.explanation: The search reads approximately half the file, and the modified page must then be written. P·D/2 alone omits that final write.

questions.prompt: Can a file sorted by x use binary search directly for y=7 merely because y is a key?
options: Yes, if y is an integer
Yes, if there is only one match
No, the search must match the file's sort order
Yes, every key can be searched by binary search
questions.explanation: Uniqueness does not make the file sorted by y. Binary search requires the relevant ordering.

questions.prompt: For P=1024 and D=2 ms, what is the approximate equality-search cost on the sort key?
options: 10 ms
20 ms
questions.explanation: The model estimates log₂1024=10 page reads. Multiplying by 2 ms per read gives 20 ms.

questions.prompt: How is a range query on a sorted key performed conceptually?
options: Locate the start of the range, then scan pages containing matches
Always read exactly one page, regardless of the range
Always scan the whole file from its beginning
Find only the final key and ignore the values in between
questions.explanation: The ordering supports locating the starting point and continuing sequentially. A wide result range can still require many pages.

questions.prompt: Why can insertion into a compact sorted file require substantial I/O?
options: Binary search is always linear
Records or pages after the insertion point may need to shift to preserve order
Every insertion changes every field type
Every insertion must build a new hash table
questions.explanation: Shifting data adds substantial cost beyond locating the insertion point. Binary search itself remains logarithmic.

questions.prompt: For P=128 and D=1 ms, use the slide's insertion formula: search + P·D. What is the approximate cost?
options: 128 ms
14 ms
135 ms
71 ms
questions.explanation: The search costs log₂128=7 ms and shifting costs 128 ms. The 71 ms option counts only half the pages without accounting for both reading and writing them.

questions.prompt: Must a search key uniquely identify every record?
options: Yes, it is always the primary key
Yes, it is always a minimal candidate key
Only when the index is a B+ tree
No, it can consist of non-unique attributes
questions.explanation: A search key identifies the field or fields used for lookup. Uniqueness is a separate property.

questions.prompt: What does an index entry contain in Variant A?
options: The record's contents
Only a (key,RID) pair
Only a (key,list of RIDs) pair
Only page-directory free-space information
questions.explanation: Variant A stores records by value. Variants B and C store references instead of the full record contents.

questions.prompt: How does Variant B differ from Variant C?
options: B is used only with hashing, while C is used only with trees
B stores one RID per entry, while C groups a key's RIDs into a list
B contains complete records, while C contains only internal pointers
B requires unique keys, while C cannot represent duplicates
questions.explanation: The difference is how references are packaged. It is independent of the index's access structure.

questions.prompt: Why can Variant C produce variable-length entries?
options: The page size changes on every lookup
A B+ tree has no leaves
Different keys can have different numbers of RIDs
Every key must be a string
questions.explanation: RID lists can have different lengths, so entry sizes can vary even when the keys have a fixed length.

questions.prompt: Why are by-reference entries useful when a table has several indexes?
options: They guarantee that key updates never need index maintenance
They automatically make every index clustered
They remove the need for a data file
They avoid repeating the entire tuple in every index
questions.explanation: RID references let multiple indexes refer to the same record. Updating an indexed key may still require index maintenance.

questions.prompt: Which index type naturally supports ranges in search-key order in this lecture?
options: A tree-based index
An ordinary hash index
Both must store keys in sorted order
Only an unindexed heap
questions.explanation: The tree structure maintains an ordering. Hashing primarily supports equality lookups and does not preserve the neighbourhood of adjacent keys.

questions.prompt: What can a hash bucket consist of?
options: Only a bitmap for the entire database
A primary page and zero or more overflow pages
Always exactly one record
Always one B+ tree root and all its leaves
questions.explanation: Overflow pages extend a bucket when necessary. A bucket is not limited to a single record.

questions.prompt: In the slides' terminology, what does a primary index's search key contain?
options: Only the root page's ID
One constant shared by every entry
The primary key
Every non-key attribute
questions.explanation: This classification depends on the search key containing the primary key. Clustering is a separate classification.

questions.prompt: Which property do the slides associate with a unique index?
options: Every entry has the same value
Every leaf contains exactly one entry
The index cannot have multiple columns
The search key contains a candidate key
questions.explanation: A candidate key guarantees uniqueness. A search key containing several columns can still be unique.

questions.prompt: Does choosing a B+ tree or a hash structure automatically determine whether entries use Variant A, B, or C?
options: No, these are independent design choices
Yes, trees can use only A
Yes, hashing can use only C
Yes, by-reference entries cannot be used with trees
questions.explanation: Entry representation is a different design choice from the tree-based or hash-based access mechanism.

questions.prompt: What relationship does a clustered index describe between data placement and index order?
options: Every leaf has only one child
Data records are kept close together in search-key order
Every record must remain in RAM
Every index key must be unique
questions.explanation: Clustering concerns the physical locality and ordering of records. It does not imply uniqueness or caching.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, how many independent search-key orders can one data file generally be clustered on at the same time?
options: As many as the number of columns, without restriction
It can never be clustered
At most one
As many as the number of records
questions.explanation: One linear physical arrangement generally cannot follow several independent orders simultaneously. Multiple unclustered indexes can still be maintained.

questions.prompt: There are 60 matching records on 3 data pages, with a cold cache. Counting only data-page retrieval, how many reads are needed?
questions.explanation: Each required data page needs to be read once. Adding an index cost to obtain 63 would introduce a cost that the question does not specify.

questions.prompt: There are 60 matching records, each on a different data page, with a cold cache. Counting only data retrieval, how many reads are needed?
options: log₂60
questions.explanation: Scattered unclustered matches can require one I/O per record. Traversing an index does not replace fetching the data pages.

questions.prompt: What is a trade-off when maintaining clustering during insertions?
options: All secondary indexes must be deleted
Free space, overflow pages, or reorganisation may be needed to preserve locality
The file never needs updating
Every insertion has zero I/O cost
questions.explanation: Maintaining physical order has a cost. Reserving space and reorganising data can help, but do not remove the trade-off entirely.
